context: a letter from Robert Swinhoe, which you are answering
exchanges:
On returning to my post at Takow after a 10 day’s revel in the heart of the Formosan Mountains, I found orders awaiting me to repair to Amoy to relieve my brother-in-law Mr. Pedder who goes home by this mail. My sister, Mrs. Pedder, has kindly offered to take home a small parcel for me. It occurred to me on her making this offer that I was under promise to procure for you some Chinese Honey-comb, or rather comb of the Chinese Honey-Bee. Enclosed in this box are several pieces of the article you desire, which my man procured after a long hunt through the town, this not being the season for gathering the honey— I hope you will be pleased with the present, and that you may find it to answer your purpose—

If you have anything further that I can assist you in, do not fail to let me know of it. Now that I am in China proper again & once more within the line of regular communication I can the more easily procure any article you desire and find opportunities for forwarding such to you—

Your’s sincerely, | Robert Swinhoe.

Cordial Thanks for so kindly remembering my wish— when I come to subject—Apis Indica—, Your kindness will lead you to be glad to hear that my health much improved, though yet far from strong— my eternal book, you a copy, if not returned before this date. I am delighted to hear that you keep on your zealous love & work for Nat History & British Assoc— New discussion—on modification of species

President’s address—   Hooker capital lecture—but I hear Wallace’s paper best—

I wish I could tell you any news, but I have not been in L. since Spring & seen nobody socially except Sir J. Lubbock—who was down chiefly comparing his collection to Archaeologs.

I suppose you see Zoolog Proc—the case of the N American antelopes so intermediate between hollow & solid-horned ruminants, is one of more curious facts I have lately heard with respect to higher animals.—
